lessons.title: My Body Parts
objectives: Name the main parts of the body
Say what some body parts help us do
prerequisites: Can point to own head, hands and feet
explanation: Our body has many parts. On top is the head, with the face: eyes to see, ears to hear, a nose to smell, and a mouth to eat and talk.
We have two arms with hands and fingers to hold, draw and wave. We have two legs with feet and toes to walk, run and jump.
Every body is different — tall, short, different colours and shapes — and every body is special.

examples: We use our hands to eat and our legs to run.

lessons.title: How I Grow
objectives: Describe ways their body has changed since being a baby
Know that growing needs food, sleep and exercise
explanation: When you were a baby, you were small and couldn't walk or talk. Now you are bigger, stronger and can do lots of things!
Your body grows slowly every day. You get taller, your feet get bigger, and one day your baby teeth will wobble and fall out so bigger teeth can grow.
To grow well, your body needs healthy food, water, lots of sleep and plenty of play and exercise.

lessons.title: My Skeleton
objectives: Name important bones: skull, ribs, spine
Explain that muscles move bones
explanation: Inside your body is a skeleton made of bones. It holds you up — without it, you'd flop like a jelly! Adults have 206 bones.
Some bones protect important organs: the skull protects your brain, and the ribs protect your heart and lungs. Your spine (backbone) lets you stand tall and bend.
Muscles are attached to bones. When a muscle pulls, the bone moves. Joints, like elbows and knees, are where bones meet and bend.

vocabulary.meaning: all the bones in your body
the bone that protects your brain
curved bones that protect your heart and lungs
a part that pulls bones to move them

examples: Feel your ribs when you breathe in.
Bend your elbow and feel the muscle in your upper arm get firm.

story.title: The Skeleton That Stood Tall
story.text: In a museum, Kiko saw a dinosaur skeleton. "It's just bones!" said Kiko. Professor Hoot smiled, "You have a skeleton too, inside. Without it, you couldn't stand. And your muscles are the ropes that pull it to make you move."

lessons.title: Listen to Your Heart
objectives: Explain that the heart pumps blood around the body
Notice that exercise makes the heart beat faster
prerequisites: Knows the ribs protect the heart
explanation: Your heart is a strong muscle about the size of your fist. It pumps blood around your whole body, day and night, without stopping.
Your lungs fill with air when you breathe in. They take oxygen from the air into your blood. When you breathe out, they push out carbon dioxide.
When you run or dance, your muscles need more oxygen, so you breathe faster and your heart beats faster. You can feel your heartbeat as a pulse in your wrist or neck.

vocabulary.meaning: a muscle that pumps blood
organs that breathe air in and out
the beat of your heart you can feel
a gas in the air our bodies need

examples: After running, your heart thumps faster.
Breathe in deeply and feel your chest get bigger.

story.title: Kiko's Thumping Drum
story.text: After racing up the hill, Kiko put a hoof on Kiko's chest. Thump-thump-thump-thump! "My heart is drumming!" Tara explained, "Your muscles need more oxygen when you run, so your heart beats faster to deliver it." After a rest, the drum slowed down again.

activities.prompt: Your heart is about the size of your fist.

thinking: Why do you breathe faster when you run?
Does your heart ever rest?
speaking: Count your heartbeats for 15 seconds before and after jumping, and tell someone what changed.

lessons.title: The Control Centre
objectives: Explain that the brain controls the body using nerves
Describe a reflex
prerequisites: Knows the skull protects the brain
explanation: Your brain is your body's control centre. It lets you think, remember, feel, and move. It is protected by your skull.

Nerves are like tiny wires that carry messages between your brain and every part of your body, very fast. When you touch something, nerves tell your brain; when you decide to wave, your brain sends a message to your arm.
A reflex is an automatic, very fast response, like pulling your hand away from something hot before you even think. Sleep helps your brain store memories and rest.

vocabulary.meaning: the organ that controls thinking and the body
a pathway carrying messages to and from the brain
an automatic quick reaction
what the brain stores to remember

examples: Blinking when something flies at your eyes is a reflex.
Learning to ride a bicycle builds new pathways in your brain.

story.title: The Message Race
story.text: Rangi touched a hot cup. Zing! A message raced up a nerve. Before Rangi even said "Ouch!", the hand had jerked away. "That was a reflex," said Nova. "Your body protected you super fast — and THEN your brain noticed."

activities.prompt: The brain is protected by the…

thinking: Why is it helpful that some reactions are automatic?

lessons.title: Bite, Tear and Chew
objectives: Name the types of teeth and their jobs
Explain how to care for teeth
explanation: You have different teeth for different jobs. Incisors at the front are flat and sharp for biting. Canines are pointy for tearing. Molars at the back are wide for chewing and grinding.
Sugary foods help germs make acid that can cause holes (cavities) in teeth. Brushing twice a day with fluoride toothpaste, for about two minutes, keeps teeth strong.
After chewing, food goes down a tube to your stomach, where it is mashed and mixed, and then into your intestines.

vocabulary.meaning: a front tooth for biting
a pointy tooth for tearing
a back tooth for chewing
a hole in a tooth caused by decay

examples: Biting an apple uses incisors.
Chewing rice uses molars.

story.title: The Sugar Bugs
story.text: Tiny germs called sugar bugs loved it when Kiko ate sticky sweets and forgot to brush. They made acid that started a little hole in a molar. Kiko visited the dentist, got it fixed, and started brushing twice a day. "No more parties for the sugar bugs!" Kiko said.

lessons.title: The Blood Highway
objectives: Describe the parts of the circulatory system
Trace blood's path through the heart, lungs and body
explanation: The circulatory system includes the heart, blood vessels and blood. Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it back. Tiny capillaries connect them and let oxygen and food pass into cells.
Humans have a double circulation: the right side of the heart pumps blood to the lungs to pick up oxygen; the left side pumps oxygen-rich blood to the whole body.
Blood contains red blood cells (carry oxygen), white blood cells (fight infection), platelets (help clotting) and plasma (the liquid that carries nutrients and wastes).

context.text: William Harvey published his demonstration of blood circulation in 1628. Earlier, Ibn al-Nafis (13th century) described the pulmonary circulation.

vocabulary.meaning: a vessel carrying blood away from the heart
a vessel carrying blood to the heart
a tiny vessel connecting arteries and veins
a cell that carries oxygen

examples: A cut stops bleeding because platelets help form a clot.
Veins look bluish through skin, but blood is always red.

story.title: Harvey's Counting
story.text: In the 1600s, William Harvey calculated how much blood the heart pumps each hour. It was far more than a body could make from food! He reasoned that the same blood must go round and round. His careful measurements overturned ideas that had been taught for centuries.

carries blood back to the heart

speaking: Trace the path of blood through the body for someone using a diagram.

lessons.title: How We Breathe
objectives: Describe the path of air into the lungs
Explain the effects of exercise and smoking on breathing
explanation: Air enters through the nose or mouth, travels down the windpipe (trachea), into two bronchi, then smaller tubes, ending in millions of tiny air sacs called alveoli. Oxygen passes from alveoli into the blood.
Breathing is powered by the diaphragm, a dome-shaped muscle under the lungs. When it contracts and flattens, the chest gets bigger and air rushes in.
Regular exercise strengthens the heart and breathing muscles. Smoking damages the alveoli and airways, making breathing harder and causing serious diseases.

vocabulary.meaning: the windpipe
tiny air sacs where oxygen enters the blood
the muscle that powers breathing
the organs used for breathing

examples: Yoga breathing (pranayama) involves slow, controlled breaths.

lessons.title: Changes During Puberty
objectives: Describe common physical and emotional changes during puberty
Explain that puberty timing varies and is normal
prerequisites: Knows the body grows and changes
explanation: Puberty is the time when a child's body begins to develop into an adult's body. It is triggered by hormones — chemical messengers in the blood. It often starts between about 8 and 14 years old and varies a lot between people.

Common changes include growth spurts, body hair, sweating more, skin changes such as pimples, voice changes, and development of the reproductive system. Girls begin menstruation (periods); boys' voices deepen.
Emotions can change too: feeling more sensitive or moody is common. Talking to trusted adults, good hygiene, sleep and healthy food all help. Everyone's timing is different — and that is normal.

vocabulary.meaning: the stage when a body develops from child to adult
a chemical messenger in the blood
a monthly period in girls and women as part of the reproductive cycle
a period of fast growth

examples: Using deodorant and bathing daily helps with extra sweat.
Some friends may grow taller earlier than others.

story.title: Different Timings
story.text: In Class 6, Riya was suddenly the tallest in her class, while her friend Meera hadn't changed at all. Meera worried something was wrong. Their teacher explained: "Everyone's body has its own timetable. Earlier or later — both are normal." Meera felt much better.

activities.prompt: Feeling more emotional during puberty is common.

thinking: Why might it help to know about puberty before it starts?

units.title: The Immune System
objectives: Describe the body's defences against pathogens
Explain how vaccines work

revision.notes: Self-test, explain the reasoning aloud, connect to other subjects, and attempt a transfer problem.

lessons.title: The Body's Defence Force
objectives: Describe the body's defences against pathogens
Explain how vaccines work
explanation: Pathogens are microbes that cause disease — some bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites. The body's first defences are barriers: skin, mucus in the nose, tears, and stomach acid.

If pathogens get in, white blood cells attack them. Some engulf pathogens; others make antibodies that lock onto specific pathogens. Memory cells remember them, so the next infection is fought off faster.

Vaccines safely train the immune system using a harmless form or part of a pathogen, so the body builds memory without getting the disease. Vaccination has greatly reduced diseases like polio — India was certified polio-free in 2014.

context.text: Edward Jenner developed the smallpox vaccine in 1796; smallpox was declared eradicated worldwide in 1980. The WHO certified India polio-free in 2014.

vocabulary.meaning: a microbe that causes disease
a protein that targets a specific pathogen
a substance that trains the immune system safely
the body's ability to resist a disease

examples: Handwashing removes pathogens before they enter the body.
Antibiotics treat bacterial infections but do not work against viruses.

story.title: The Last Case of Smallpox
story.text: Smallpox once killed millions of people. Through a huge global vaccination effort — including mass campaigns in India in the 1970s — health workers tracked down every case. The last naturally occurring case was in 1977, and in 1980 the world declared smallpox eradicated. It is one of humanity's greatest achievements.

activities.prompt: Memory cells help the body fight an infection faster the second time.

thinking: Why do some vaccines need booster doses?
Why is vaccinating many people important even for those who can't be vaccinated?
speaking: Explain to someone how a vaccine works using the idea of a "wanted poster".

revision.notes: Spaced retrieval with written explanations, peer-teaching, and an extension question each cycle.

lessons.title: Keeping Balance
objectives: Explain homeostasis and negative feedback
Describe control of body temperature and blood glucose
explanation: Homeostasis is keeping conditions inside the body stable — temperature around 37 °C, blood glucose and water levels within safe ranges — even when the outside changes.

It works by negative feedback: a change is detected, and the body responds to reverse it. If you overheat, you sweat and blood vessels near the skin widen to lose heat; if cold, you shiver and vessels narrow.

Blood glucose is controlled by hormones from the pancreas. After a meal, insulin helps cells take in glucose, lowering blood sugar. In type 1 diabetes, the body makes little or no insulin; in type 2, the body doesn't respond to insulin properly.

vocabulary.meaning: maintaining a stable internal environment
a response that reverses a change
a hormone that lowers blood glucose
an organ that makes insulin

examples: Shivering generates heat from muscle activity.
Diabetes affects millions of people in India.

story.title: The Discovery of Insulin
story.text: In 1921–22, Frederick Banting, Charles Best and colleagues in Toronto extracted insulin and used it to treat a 14-year-old boy, Leonard Thompson, who was dying of diabetes. He recovered. Insulin turned a fatal disease into a manageable condition for millions.

thinking: Why is negative feedback a good design for keeping things stable?
How can lifestyle affect the risk of type 2 diabetes?
speaking: Explain temperature control to someone, using a home thermostat as an analogy.

lessons.title: Is This Health Claim True?
objectives: Evaluate health claims using evidence
Explain how clinical trials test treatments
prerequisites: Understands body systems and the immune system
explanation: Health claims are everywhere — in adverts, social media and messages forwarded by relatives. Some are helpful, some are wrong, and some are dangerous.

Good evidence often comes from randomised controlled trials: participants are randomly split into groups, one receiving the treatment and one a placebo or standard care, often without knowing which (blinding). This shows whether the treatment itself works.
Ask: Who is making the claim? Is there evidence from trials? Is it a single story or many patients? Does it promise a "miracle cure"? Check with qualified doctors and reliable health organisations.

vocabulary.meaning: a study testing a medical treatment on people
an inactive treatment used for comparison
assigned by chance
false or misleading information

examples: "This herb cures all diseases" — a red-flag claim.
A vaccine approved after large phase 3 trials.

story.title: James Lind and the Oranges
story.text: In 1747, ship's surgeon James Lind tested treatments for scurvy on twelve sick sailors, giving pairs different remedies. Those given oranges and lemons recovered fast. It was one of the first controlled trials — and showed the power of comparing treatments fairly.

activities.prompt: Randomisation helps make trial groups fair.

thinking: Why are personal stories not enough to prove a treatment works?
How should you respond kindly when a relative forwards a false health message?
speaking: Evaluate a real health advert or message with someone, explaining your reasoning.

steps: Choose a claim

assessment.prompt: The strongest evidence for a treatment usually comes from…
